Representative_Docs: ["The Recruitment (or precisely, the recruiters!) is a nightmare here! The Recruitment team is so lethargic and the processes are such a mess! From a candidate's perspective, if there's an Opening to which the profile of the candidate is a 100% match, he will still be unsure if a recruiter actually gets to look at it. There are so many channels for putting the Open positions - through LinkedIn, Naukri, IIImJObs as well as Agencies, that even recruiters can't manage properly. From the companies side, it is always hard to find the right candidate, all thanks to recruitment team and process, and even if a candidate is found, the onboarding Process takes ages! In many cases, the candidate either gets another offer or ends up following with the recruiters for initiating the onboarding himself! All in all, there is no Morale check of potential joiners, salary negotiations are very stringent so much so that they even bargain for a mere 5%.", 'Underpaid compares to market, Associates get paid $35K more per year but do the same amount of work/same difficulty of work. Too much focus on diversity, people do not get promoted for the right reasons. NY teams look down on you, management is hit or miss. Retention is terrible, so much that you have to work excessive hours to make up for lack of staff.', 'So many meetings. Why does every meeting need 18 men in a room shouting at each other? Diversity is good but remember JPMC is a global company so there will be culture clash. You know how somebody from Jersey and someone from California will probably have some miscommunication even though they’re both American? Well this will be amplified 10-fold when you’re at a global company. You will probably have a lot of remote meetings at random times with people across the globe. Moreover, there doesn’t seem to be a huge push for diversity and the majority of tech is the same majorities you seem to see at tech companies, and if you’re American of any race you’ll probably be in the minority. And remember, non-Americans haven’t confronted issues about race/ethnicity or as long as other countries, so prepare to hear some random tone-deaf remarks from immigrant coworkers (nothing mean per se, just tone-deaf). The Seattle branch is facing the same issue that most non-Amazon companies face: every employee tends to be ex-Amazon and thus the new company becomes little Amazon. Recruiters love to reach out to Amazonians because they don’t know how the sausage is made, but those that are on the inside know they bring a certain Type-A culture and letting themselves be overworked. Moreover, recruiters assume Amazon experience == AWS experience, but really the non-Amazonians I’ve worked with had more hands-on AWS knowledge. It is still a top-down culture so there will be times when some random higher-up you’ve never met in person and is probably across the globe mandates an initiative with an arbitrary deadline. Health/dental are overpriced. No benefits like orca card yet. Like a month of PTO depending on level. Moreover, the dev environment is so locked down due to “security reasons”, which is fair. However, it means you’ll be using dated technology and if JPMC really cared about development experience, they’d spend some of that $9b quarterly profit to hire more security folk to help the developers get a modern experience to develop more business value. Instead, you’re between a rock and a hard place of getting arbitrary deadlines with so much red tape and so many meetings. Hard pass especially in Seattle where there are so many more fast-paced environments. I’m all about company for a couple of years at least but it was extremely difficult to stay longer than a year at a company with so many meetings, so much red tape, so little development, and so bad for the resume, especially in Seattle where complacency is killer. Unless you’re hired for a very specific team and a very specific project that’ll perfectly align with your career goals, i would say don’t bother.']
